newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-"Bad Religion" show punks get angrier as they get older.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-"Bad Religion" show punks get angrier as they get older.

text.p: Almost by definition, punk rock bands consist of angry young renegades who preach anarchy, demolition and damnation before quickly self-destructing to become pop culture symbols.
But what if a punk band doesn't go the way of the Germs, the Clash or the Sex Pistols and goes on releasing albums? Can its members still be rock 'n' outlaws in their 30s?
Bad Religion, which formed in southern California not long after the Sex Pistols broke up almost 20 years ago, are proving that time only makes them more angry and more punk.

Despite some recent upheavals, the band has remained true to its ethos as it makes records and plays to fans around the world. It toured the world for much of the year to promote its latest album, "The Gray Race" (Atlantic), and has just begun another U.S. leg.

"We're somewhat below the mainstream and I like being there, because being as popular as Green Day or the Offspring is a huge burden and we're very fortunate to not have that burden and yet still enjoy the benefits of being looked at ... as a band with a lot of influence," Greg Graffin, the band's vocalist and songwriter, told Reuters.

Of course, there are some differences between then and now. The schoolboys from the neatly manicured Los Angeles suburb of Woodland Hills are now family men spread across North America. Perhaps more importantly, Bad Religion is adjusting to life without guitarist and founding member Brett Gurewitz, who resigned in 1994 to run his multi-million-dollar recording empire. This allowed Graffin, a Ph.D candidate on the evolution of bone tissue, to take creative control.

"The Gray Race" is also the band's second album released solely by Atlantic, a major label that signed the group in 1993. The deal immediately aroused controversy among fans and critics who accused the band of selling out its rich heritage as an independent. Although major labels account for most hard rock sales, Bad Religion's move was seen as plain sacrilege.

Graffin dismisses the critics as people more interested in trends than in music. "Ever since we were kids, when we started the band, we always said, 'This isn't about fashion, this is about music, the ideas,'" he said.

"The 'repeat customers' are those who are interested in the new ideas or the way we say our old ideas and in the excitement of the music. They don't care who's marketing it, and they don't care how popular 'Bad Religion' is."

Despite the distractions, the sound of "The Gray Race," its ninth album, is not much different from previous efforts. Brian Baker, formerly with thrash band Minor Threat, replaces Gurewitz, joining bass player Jay Bentley, guitarist Greg Hetson and drummer Bobby Schayer.

The album underscores the band's passion for combining hard-charging music with thought-provoking lyrics that defy rules of meter and often call for a dictionary. For example "Them and Us" is about the futility of stereotyping people.

Graffin, the son of an English teacher, said, "A lot of people, I think, have a stereotyped view of rock music, especially punk music, that at that speed you can't get out any complex thoughts. But I wanted to really prove to people that not only is it an infectious kind of beat but you can also put out pretty complex thoughts behind it."
"The Gray Race" also dwells on such topics as Malthusian economics ("Ten in 2010") and the dilemmas facing the human race (the title track).

Graffin, 31, who now lives with his family in upstate New York, says he is more eager to broach such issues as he gets older. "The more I travel, the more I see and study the human race, the more that I feel justified in the issues that I bring up. I'm more determined and more staunch."
